data.title: Safety and efficacy of tolebrutinib, an oral brain-penetrant BTK inhibitor, in relapsing multiple sclerosis: a phase 2b, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Tolebrutinib is an oral, CNS-penetrant, irreversible inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase, an enzyme expressed in B lymphocytes and myeloid cells including microglia, which are major drivers of inflammation in multiple sclerosis. We aimed to determine the dose-response relationship between tolebrutinib and the reduction in new active brain MRI lesions in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis.
METHODS
We did a 16-week, phase 2b, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover, dose-finding trial at 40 centres (academic sites, specialty clinics, and general neurology centres) in ten countries in Europe and North America. Eligible participants were adults aged 18-55 years with diagnosed relapsing multiple sclerosis (either relapsing-remitting or relapsing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis), and one or more of the following criteria: at least one relapse within the previous year, at least two relapses within the previous 2 years, or at least one active gadolinium-enhancing brain lesion in the 6 months before screening. Exclusion criteria included a diagnosis of primary progressive multiple sclerosis or a diagnosis of secondary progressive multiple sclerosis without relapse. We used a two-step randomisation process to randomly assign eligible participants (1:1) to two cohorts, then further randomly assign participants in each cohort (1:1:1:1) to four tolebrutinib dose groups (5, 15, 30, and 60 mg administered once daily as an oral tablet). Cohort 1 received tolebrutinib for 12 weeks, then matched placebo (ie, identical looking tablets) for 4 weeks; cohort 2 received 4 weeks of placebo followed by 12 weeks of tolebrutinib. Participants and investigators were masked for dose and tolebrutinib-placebo administration sequence; investigators, study team members, and study participants did not have access to unmasked data. MRI scans were done at screening and every 4 weeks over 16 weeks. The primary efficacy endpoint was the number of new gadolinium-enhancing lesions detected on the scan done after 12 weeks of tolebrutinib treatment (assessed at week 12 for cohort 1 and week 16 for cohort 2), relative to the scan done 4 weeks previously, and compared with the lesions accumulated during 4 weeks of placebo run-in period in cohort 2. Efficacy data were analysed in a modified intention-to-treat population, using a two-step multiple comparison procedure with modelling analysis. Safety was assessed for all participants who received at least one dose of study drug. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03889639), EudraCT (2018-003927-12), and WHO (U1111-1220-0572), and has been completed.
FINDINGS
Between May 14, 2019, and Jan 2, 2020, we enrolled and randomly assigned 130 participants to tolebrutinib: 33 to 5 mg, 32 to 15 mg, 33 to 30 mg, and 32 to 60 mg. 129 (99%) completed the treatment regimen and 126 were included in the primary analysis. At treatment week 12, there was a dose-dependent reduction in the number of new gadolinium-enhancing lesions (mean [SD] lesions per patient: placebo, 1·03 [2·50]; 5 mg, 1·39 [3·20]; 15 mg, 0·77 [1·48]; 30 mg, 0·76 [3·31]; 60 mg, 0·13 [0·43]; p=0·03). One serious adverse event was reported (one patient in the 60 mg group was admitted to hospital because of a multiple sclerosis relapse). The most common non-serious adverse event during tolebrutinib treatment was headache (in one [3%] of 33 in the 5 mg group; three [9%] of 32 in the 15 mg group; one [3%] of 33 in the 30 mg group; and four [13%] of 32 in the 60 mg group). No safety-related discontinuations or treatment-related deaths occurred.
INTERPRETATION
12 weeks of tolebrutinib treatment led to a dose-dependent reduction in new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, the 60 mg dose being the most efficacious, and the drug was well tolerated. Reduction of acute inflammation, combined with the potential to modulate the immune response within the CNS, provides a scientific rationale to pursue phase 3 clinical trials of tolebrutinib in patients with relapsing and progressive forms of multiple sclerosis.

Sanofi.

data.title: Safety and efficacy of evobrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis (evolutionRMS1 and evolutionRMS2): two multicentre, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled, phase 3 trials.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Bottom line

- In progressive multiple sclerosis (MS), the most mature randomized evidence for Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors comes from tolebrutinib in nonrelapsing secondary progressive MS (SPMS), where disability progression was reduced versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.55–0.88), with a higher rate of ALT elevations >3×ULN in the tolebrutinib arm. This directly addresses disability accrual, a key endpoint in progressive MS. <cite id="40202696">In participants with nonrelapsing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, the risk of disability progression was lower among those who received treatment with tolebrutinib than among those who received placebo (22.6% vs. 30.7%; hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% confidence interval, 0.55 to 0.88; P = 0.003), though more had ALT increases >3×ULN with tolebrutinib (4.0% vs. 1.6%).</cite>

- For MRI outcomes, BTK inhibition has shown effects on acute lesion activity in relapsing MS, but head-to-head randomized data in progressive, nonrelapsing disease are limited. Tolebrutinib in relapsing cohorts demonstrated a dose-dependent reduction in new gadolinium-enhancing lesions at 12 weeks, with the 60 mg dose most efficacious, supporting CNS penetration and immunomodulatory activity; however, this was not a progressive, nonrelapsing population. <cite id="34418400">In a 16-week crossover trial in relapsing MS, 12 weeks of tolebrutinib led to a dose-dependent reduction in new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, with 60 mg being the most efficacious (mean lesions per patient: placebo 1.03; 60 mg 0.13; p=0.03).</cite> Evobrutinib and fenebrutinib trials in relapsing MS show mixed or nonsuperior efficacy versus active comparators and do not answer the progressive, nonrelapsing question. <cite id="39307151">Evobrutinib was not superior to teriflunomide in relapsing MS, with higher rates of serious TEAEs and liver enzyme elevations, particularly in the first 12 weeks.</cite> <cite id="40683275">Fenebrutinib reduced new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions by 69% over weeks 4–12 versus placebo in relapsing MS and was well tolerated, but its impact on progressive, nonrelapsing disability progression remains unproven.</cite> <cite id="38436271">Long-term evobrutinib treatment in relapsing MS maintained low disease activity and CNS exposure, but efficacy in progressive, nonrelapsing disability progression is not established.</cite>

# Evidence by agent

- Tolebrutinib (oral, CNS-penetrant BTK inhibitor)
  - Progressive (nonrelapsing) MS: Disability progression (sustained 6 months) reduced vs placebo (22.6% vs 30.7%; HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.55–0.88; P=0.003) in a phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=1131). Adverse events: serious AE rates 15.0% vs 10.4%; ALT >3×ULN 4.0% vs 1.6%. <cite id="40202696">In participants with nonrelapsing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, the risk of disability progression was lower among those who received treatment with tolebrutinib than among those who received placebo (22.6% vs. 30.7%; hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% confidence interval, 0.55 to 0.88; P = 0.003), with higher ALT elevations in the tolebrutinib group.</cite>
  - Relapsing MS (MRI activity): Dose-dependent reduction in new gadolinium-enhancing lesions at 12 weeks, with 60 mg most effective, supporting CNS action. <cite id="34418400">At week 12, new gadolinium-enhancing lesions decreased in a dose-dependent manner with tolebrutinib, reaching 0.13 lesions per patient at 60 mg versus 1.03 with placebo (p=0.03).</cite>

- Evobrutinib (oral, CNS-penetrant, selective BTK inhibitor)
  - Relapsing MS (MRI and disability): In two phase 3 trials versus teriflunomide, annualized relapse rates were similar and evobrutinib showed no superiority; liver enzyme elevations and serious TEAEs were more frequent, especially early on. <cite id="39307151">Annualized relapse rates favored neither drug in the pooled analysis, while serious TEAEs and liver enzyme elevations (≥5×ULN) were more common with evobrutinib; cases meeting Hy's law resolved after discontinuation.</cite>
  - Long-term safety and disease activity: Sustained low disease activity and stable EDSS with evobrutinib over >3.5 years, but this was in relapsing MS populations and not progressive, nonrelapsing disability progression. <cite id="38436271">Long-term evobrutinib treatment maintained low annualized relapse rates (0.11 at week 48; 0.11 at week 192), stable EDSS, and low T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesion numbers, with CSF detection of drug.</cite>

- Fenebrutinib (highly selective, reversible BTK inhibitor)
  - Relapsing MS (MRI): Strong reduction in new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions versus placebo over weeks 4–12 (69% relative reduction), with favorable tolerability in a 12-week phase 2 trial; ongoing studies are exploring progressive MS. <cite id="40683275">The combined number of new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions at weeks 4, 8, and 12 was 0.077 in the fenebrutinib group vs 0.245 in placebo (69% relative reduction; p=0.0022), with no serious adverse events during the double-blind phase.</cite>

# What this means for progressive MS

- Disability outcomes: The only direct head-to-head evidence in progressive, nonrelapsing disease is tolebrutinib, which reduced confirmed disability progression sustained for 6 months versus placebo, suggesting a potential role for BTK inhibition in slowing disability accrual when relapses are absent. <cite id="40202696">Tolebrutinib reduced the risk of sustained 6-month disability progression compared with placebo in nonrelapsing secondary progressive MS (HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.55–0.88).</cite>

- MRI chronic active lesions: In progressive, nonrelapsing disease, chronic active lesions are typically non-enhancing; mature randomized data for BTK inhibitors on chronic lesion reduction are lacking. Indirectly, BTK inhibitors reduce new enhancing lesions in relapsing MS, supporting activity against inflammatory components, but chronic lesion modification has not been conclusively demonstrated in progressive cohorts. <cite id="34418400">Tolebrutinib reduced new gadolinium-enhancing lesions in relapsing MS in a dose-dependent manner, supporting anti-inflammatory activity within the CNS.</cite> <cite id="40683275">Fenebrutinib also reduced new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions by 69% over weeks 4–12 versus placebo in relapsing MS, but evidence in progressive, nonrelapsing disease is limited.</cite>

# Safety considerations

- Liver enzyme elevations: Across BTK inhibitors, ALT/AST elevations (including ≥5×ULN) have been reported more frequently than with placebo/active comparators, particularly early with evobrutinib; monitoring and risk mitigation are important. <cite id="39307151">Liver enzyme elevations at least 5×ULN were more common with evobrutinib, especially in the first 12 weeks, with cases meeting Hy's law resolving after discontinuation.</cite> <cite id="40202696">ALT levels >3×ULN occurred more often with tolebrutinib than placebo in nonrelapsing SPMS.</cite>

- Overall tolerability: Tolebrutinib and fenebrutinib trials reported acceptable safety with no excess serious adverse events in relapsing MS; evobrutinib showed nonsuperior efficacy and more frequent liver-related adverse events. <cite id="40683275">Fenebrutinib was well tolerated in relapsing MS with no serious adverse events in the double-blind phase.</cite> <cite id="38436271">Long-term evobrutinib was well tolerated with sustained low disease activity and CSF exposure.</cite>

# Practical interpretation

- For progressive MS without relapses, current randomized evidence supports tolebrutinib as the most promising BTK inhibitor, reducing sustained disability progression versus placebo, but data on reducing chronic, non-enhancing lesions are limited. <cite id="40202696">Tolebrutinib reduced sustained disability progression in nonrelapsing SPMS versus placebo.</cite>

- For MRI measures of chronic active lesions (typically non-enhancing), BTK inhibitors have not yet demonstrated clear benefits in progressive, nonrelapsing disease; their proven value lies in reducing new enhancing lesions in relapsing MS, suggesting anti-inflammatory activity that may indirectly influence progression. <cite id="34418400">Tolebrutinib reduced new gadolinium-enhancing lesions in relapsing MS in a dose-dependent manner.</cite> <cite id="40683275">Fenebrutinib similarly reduced new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions versus placebo in relapsing MS.</cite>

- Given mixed results and safety profiles across agents, treatment decisions should weigh the demonstrated benefit on disability accrual (tolebrutinib) against risks such as liver enzyme elevations and uncertain MRI benefits in progressive, nonrelapsing disease. <cite id="40202696">Tolebrutinib reduced disability progression but increased ALT elevations >3×ULN compared with placebo.</cite> <cite id="39307151">Evobrutinib showed no superiority to teriflunomide and had more frequent liver-related adverse events.</cite>

# Key uncertainties

- Lack of head-to-head randomized trials in progressive, nonrelapsing MS limits firm conclusions on comparative efficacy across BTK inhibitors.
- Evidence on reducing non-enhancing chronic lesions (hallmark of progressive MS) with BTK inhibitors remains indirect and insufficient; longer-duration imaging outcomes and disability endpoints in progressive populations are needed.
